text:
[ Khāṇḍavadahana Parva | Chapter 227 | 228 | ] || Ādiparva ||

Arjuna, highly incensed, struck down that rain with his arrows <note>the text refers to the rain of arrows as "a rain," metaphorically linked to Indra's power</note>. Seeing that rain being made fruitless, the <term>Śatakratu</term> <gloss>the hundred-sacrificed one (Indra)</gloss>, the <term>Pākaśāsana</term> <gloss>the subduer of the demon Pāka (Indra)</gloss>, increased that rain even more.
That <term>Pākaśāsana</term> <gloss>Indra</gloss> created a downpour of arrows of great speed, and he (Arjuna) made it dissolve, gladdening the others in the same way. <margin>828</margin>
<margin>Paya</margin> Then, raising a great peak of Mount <term>Mandara</term> <gloss>a mythical mountain</gloss> in his hands, complete with trees, he cast it down, desiring to kill the son of <term>Pāṇḍu</term> <gloss>Arjuna</gloss>.
Then, with arrows that were swift and had flaming tips, Arjuna shattered the mountain peak into a thousand pieces.
The appearance of that mountain being shattered shone then like the sky breaking apart along with its sun, moon, and planets.
By that huge mountain falling upon the forest, the creatures living in <term>Khāṇḍava</term> <gloss>a legendary forest</gloss> were destroyed there.
Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-seventh chapter of the <term>Khāṇḍavadahana Parva</term> <gloss>the chapter on the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest</gloss> in the <term>Ādiparva</term> <gloss>the first book</gloss>, regarding the battle between the gods, Kṛṣṇa, and Arjuna. || 227 ||
|| <term>Vaiśampāyana</term> <gloss>a sage and narrator</gloss> said || Terrified by the fall of that mountain, the inhabitants of <term>Khāṇḍava</term>—the <term>Dānavas</term> <gloss>demons</gloss>, <term>Rākṣasas</term> <gloss>man-eating demons</gloss>, <term>Nāgas</term> <gloss>serpent beings</gloss>, and the tree-dwelling creatures—<margin>829</margin>
Elephants in rut, tigers, and maned lions, all distraught, abandoned their own kind, and all species of beings.
They gazed upon that forest, angry and with weapons raised, and it stood as if agitated by the sound of the collapse.
Seeing the forest burning in many places, and <term>Kṛṣṇa</term> with his weapon raised, they let out a fierce cry.
By that fierce cry and by the roar of the Fire-god <note>original: "vibhāvasoḥ" (of the Fire god)</note>, the whole sky rumbled as if with storm clouds.
Then, for the destruction of them, the long-armed <term>Keśava</term> <gloss>Kṛṣṇa</gloss> released his extremely fierce, bright as the light of the sun and radiant discus <term>cakra</term>. <margin>830</margin>
Struck by that, the lesser beings, along with the <term>Dānavas</term> and <term>Niśācaras</term> <gloss>night-wanderers/demons</gloss>, were severed in the hundreds and fell into the fire in an instant.
There, those <term>Daityas</term> <gloss>demons</gloss>, torn apart by Kṛṣṇa’s discus and covered in fat and blood, looked like storm clouds at twilight.
Slaughtering the <term>Piśācas</term> <gloss>flesh-eating demons</gloss>, the glowing <term>Nāgas</term>, and the animals by the thousands, the <term>Vārṣṇeya</term> <gloss>Kṛṣṇa (of the Vṛṣṇi clan)</gloss> moved about like Death itself, O descendant of <term>Bharata</term> <gloss>a title for the listener, Janamejaya</gloss>.
Wondrous, wondrous was the discus of Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of foes; having severed many creatures, it returns to his hand again and again.
As he slaughtered the <term>Piśācas</term>, serpents, and <term>Rākṣasas</term> in this way, the appearance of the one who is the soul of all beings became most fierce. <margin>831</margin>
Among all the gathered gods, there was no one who could conquer Kṛṣṇa and the son of <term>Pāṇḍu</term> in battle.
When the gods could not protect their own force or extinguish that forest, they turned away.
Seeing the gods turn away, <term>Śatakratu</term> <gloss>Indra</gloss>, the hundred-sacrificed one, became joyful, O King, praising <term>Keśava</term> <gloss>Kṛṣṇa</gloss> and <term>Arjuna</term>.
When the gods had retreated, a disembodied voice spoke, addressing <term>Śatakratu</term> with a deep, grave sound.
Your friend, the excellent serpent <term>Takṣaka</term>, is not present; at the time of the burning of <term>Khāṇḍava</term>, he had gone to <term>Kurukṣetra</term>. <margin>832</margin>
And these two, <term>Vāsudeva</term> <gloss>Kṛṣṇa</gloss> and <term>Arjuna</term>, cannot be conquered in battle by any means, O <term>Vāsava</term> <gloss>Indra</gloss>; understand this from my words.
These two are <term>Nara</term> and <term>Nārāyaṇa</term>, the ancient gods known in heaven. You yourself know their strength and prowess.
These two, who are difficult to assail and unconquerable in battle, cannot be defeated—even among all the worlds, they are the most excellent of ancient sages.
They are most worthy of worship by all: gods, demons, <term>Yakṣas</term>, <term>Rākṣasas</term>, <term>Gandharvas</term>, humans, <term>Kinnaras</term>, and <term>Pannagas</term> <gloss>serpents</gloss>.
Therefore, O <term>Vāsava</term> <gloss>Indra</gloss>, you should depart from here along with the gods. Observe that the destruction of <term>Khāṇḍava</term> is destined. <margin>833</margin>
Having heard this statement and realizing it was the truth, the lord of the immortals set aside his anger and resentment and departed for heaven.

<summary>This passage details the battle during the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest, where Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna defeat the gods and their forces, ultimately leading Indra to accept their superior power and withdraw.</summary>
<keywords>Khāṇḍavadahana, Arjuna, Kṛṣṇa, Indra, Nara-Nārāyaṇa, Battle of Khāṇḍava</keywords>
